passage: Bhavna stopped Minakshi outside the Class 5 door in Pune with a loud whisper. "Is it true you go to the special reading class because you can't read properly?" A few heads turned. Minakshi's cheeks burned, and for a second she wanted to run to the toilets. It was partly true: on Tuesdays and Fridays she did go for extra help with reading. She took a slow breath. "Yes, I go for extra reading help," she said evenly. "It's private, though, so let's not talk about it." Bhavna shrugged. "Oh. Okay." The little crowd drifted off toward the swings. Minakshi's hands still trembled, but her shoulders felt lighter than they had all morning.

qa.q: On which days does Minakshi go for extra help with reading?
qa.a: On Tuesdays and Fridays.

qa.q: What was Minakshi feeling when her cheeks burned, and what changed after she answered?
qa.a: She felt shame and wanted to run away; after saying it calmly, her shoulders felt lighter.

qa.q: What could Minakshi do if the talk starts again?
qa.a: She can say calmly that yes, it is true but private, and tell a teacher if the teasing keeps going.

qa.q: How might Bhavna see Minakshi's calm answer?
qa.a: Bhavna shrugged and said "Oh. Okay," which suggests the calm answer left her with nothing more to whisper about.

grounding: A rumour holds a grain of truth and the child feels shame, then calmly owns it, says it is private and ends the talk.

passage: I'm Lakshmi, and last month our school cricket team lost the final by two runs. I sat on the boundary rope and cried into my knees; my throat felt tight. I had cared so much. After a while I wiped my face, walked over to Sangeeta, the other captain, and said, "Well played." She hugged me quickly. On the way home I thought about how slow I am running between the wickets. I didn't throw my bat or blame the umpire, though for one minute I wanted to. Next week I will practise my running.

qa.q: By how many runs did Lakshmi's team lose the final?
qa.a: By two runs.

qa.q: What was Lakshmi feeling as she sat crying on the boundary rope?
qa.a: Crushed: she had cared so much, and her throat felt tight.

qa.q: What could Lakshmi practise next?
qa.a: Her running between the wickets.

qa.q: How might Sangeeta have felt when Lakshmi said "Well played"?
qa.a: Probably appreciated, since she hugged Lakshmi quickly.

grounding: A child loses the final and is crushed, cries, congratulates the winners and decides what to practise.

passage: In the school gym the final whistle blew, and Gopika's house had lost 12-14 after a foul on her was not called. In the handshake line she kept her arms crossed and skipped the winners' hands, jaw clenched. Later, by the notice board, she kept replaying that last minute. Arnab Sir found her. "You look like you have something to say." She said, quietly, "Sir, I think the last foul was missed." He listened. "Maybe it was. Referees make mistakes. I'll mention it, but the result stands." Gopika let out a long breath. Next morning she found the winning captain and said, stiffly, "Well played."

qa.q: What was the score when Gopika's house lost?
qa.a: It lost 12-14.

qa.q: What was Gopika feeling about the last foul, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Bitter and unfairly treated: she crossed her arms, clenched her jaw and kept replaying the missed foul.

qa.q: What small step would help Gopika let go after the talk with the coach?
qa.a: Congratulating the winning captain, even if stiffly, and putting her energy into the next practice.

qa.q: How might Arnab Sir see Gopika's complaint?
qa.a: He listened and said referees make mistakes, so he probably sees a fair concern from a disappointed player, though he knows the result stands.

grounding: A child thinks the other team won unfairly, first refuses handshakes, then speaks politely to the coach and moves on.

passage:
Friday. Kashish packed her racket bag for the table-tennis final and told her mother, "Win or lose, I'll shake hands." Her stomach fluttered anyway.

Saturday. She lost to Sachin, three games to one. Her eyes stung and her legs felt heavy. She walked around the table, held out her hand and said, "Well played." It was hard to say. Sachin grinned, surprised. "Thanks. Your last serve was really tricky."

Monday. In class, two friends and even the sports teacher nodded at her. Kashish still felt a little sore about the loss, but steady too. At recess she asked Sachin to show her his backhand.

qa.q: Who did Kashish play in the table-tennis final?
qa.a: She played Sachin.

qa.q: What was Kashish feeling as she held out her hand to Sachin?
qa.a: It was hard for her, since her eyes stung and her legs felt heavy, but she still said "Well played."

qa.q: What could Kashish do next to improve after the loss?
qa.a: Learn from Sachin, for example by asking him to show his backhand, and keep practising.

qa.q: How might Sachin have felt when Kashish shook his hand?
qa.a: Surprised and pleased: he grinned and praised her last serve.

grounding: A child loses and still shakes hands and says well played, earning respect while accepting that wins and losses pass.

passage: Note, Friday, from Dolma (PE teacher). After the district football semi-final loss, the head coach spoke loudly to the team for a long while. Sahil, age 10, stood at the back with his eyes on his boots and his shoulders up near his ears. When asked why he missed the pass, he said nothing. Afterwards he sat on the bench and told me quietly that he felt small. I said the points about passing and positions were worth remembering, but the loud tone was not a measure of him. We wrote down two points together. I told him that if anyone ever makes him truly scared or hurt, he should tell his parents. I will also speak to the head coach about the tone.

qa.q: How old is Sahil?
qa.a: He is 10.

qa.q: What does Sahil's posture and silence suggest about how he felt after the loss?
qa.a: That he felt scared and small: his eyes were on his boots, his shoulders were up, and he told Dolma quietly that he felt small.

qa.q: How could Sahil separate the useful points from the harsh tone?
qa.a: By writing down the points about passing and positions, as they did together, and letting the loud tone go.

qa.q: How might the head coach see the situation?
qa.a: Probably as wanting the team to improve after a loss, though Dolma plans to speak to them because the tone left a child scared.

grounding: A coach is angry after a loss and the child feels scared and small; a teacher notes the useful points, separates the tone and reminds him to tell parents.

passage: Jeevan, come here. Old Anirban lost a badminton final at eleven, and I want to tell you what my father said in the car. "You should have won. You had him." I stared out at the wet road. I felt I had let him down, and I hardly noticed my sore hand. Then I said, in a small voice, "I did my best, Papa. I need you on my side, not more pushing." He was quiet for a whole traffic light. Then he said, "Hm. Maybe I wanted that trophy more than you did." He bought us hot jalebis. He isn't perfect, Jeevan, but he heard me.

qa.q: What did Anirban's father say in the car?
qa.a: "You should have won. You had him."

qa.q: What was Anirban feeling as he stared at the wet road?
qa.a: That he had let his father down, so he felt hurt and disappointed.

qa.q: What could a child say to a parent who piles on pressure after a loss?
qa.a: That they did their best and need support, not more pressure, as Anirban did.

qa.q: How might Anirban's father have felt after hearing him?
qa.a: Thoughtful and a bit sorry, since he was quiet for a whole traffic light, admitted he may have wanted the trophy more and bought jalebis. 🙂

grounding: An elder recalls a father saying you should have won, and how telling him he did his best and needed support changed the moment.

passage:
Tuesday. After the relay race was lost by a hair, Pranav said loudly, "It's Vidya's leg. She's slow." Vidya's face fell. Pranav felt relieved for a moment, as if the loss now belonged to someone else.

Thursday. Replaying the race in his head, he counted his own dropped baton at the first exchange and another teammate's late start. His neck went warm. Blaming Vidya had been easy, but it wasn't the whole truth.

Friday. At practice he said, "I shouldn't have said that. Our handovers were messy, mine too. Want to practise them together?" Vidya nodded slowly and picked up the baton.

qa.q: What did Pranav say about Vidya after the relay?
qa.a: He said, "It's Vidya's leg. She's slow."

qa.q: What did Pranav feel right after blaming Vidya, and what did he feel later?
qa.a: Relief at first, as if the loss belonged to someone else; later his neck went warm as he saw his own mistakes.

qa.q: What could the team do to improve for the next race?
qa.a: Practise baton handovers together, since the exchanges were messy for several runners, not only Vidya.

qa.q: How might Vidya feel when Pranav offers to practise handovers?
qa.a: She may still feel hurt, but her slow nod and picking up the baton suggest she is willing to trust him a little.

grounding: A child blames the slower teammate for a loss, feels brief relief, then sees his own part and encourages her instead.

passage:
Sunday night. Dear diary, today I dropped an easy catch in the last over and we lost the match. I wanted to dig a hole in the ground. Nitin muttered, "Great job," and looked away. My eyes stung all the way to the bus. Then Diya sat next to me and said, "Everyone drops one. I dropped two last week." She shared her orange slices. My chest felt looser. If everyone was like Nitin, I would be scared to even hold a ball. Tomorrow I will go to practice and take catches. Maybe.

- Varun

qa.q: What did Diya say to Varun on the bus?
qa.a: She said, "Everyone drops one. I dropped two last week."

qa.q: How did Varun feel after Diya spoke, and what does it change for him?
qa.a: His chest felt looser, and he is ready to try again, since he plans to go to practice and take catches.

qa.q: How could Varun get his confidence back at practice?
qa.a: By taking catches one at a time with kind teammates like Diya beside him. 🙂

qa.q: What might Diya be trying to do when she says she dropped two last week?
qa.a: Show that dropping a catch is normal, so Varun does not feel alone or scared to play.

grounding: A child drops the catch and the team loses; a friend's kindness that everyone drops one lets him try again, unlike Nitin's harsh reaction.

passage: I'm Aditi, and on Saturday our school football team beat Ishita's team 2-1. I scored the winning goal. I felt like I was floating and wanted to shout it from the roof. But then I saw Ishita, their goalkeeper, sitting on the grass with her gloves in her lap. I remembered how it felt when we lost last year. So I hugged my teammates, thanked our defenders, and went over to say, "You saved so many shots, Ishita." She almost smiled. I'm still proud, but I'm glad I didn't do a victory dance in front of her.

qa.q: Who scored the winning goal?
qa.a: Aditi scored it.

qa.q: What was Aditi thinking when she saw Ishita sitting on the grass?
qa.a: She remembered how it felt to lose last year, so she realised Ishita felt bad and wanted to be kind.

qa.q: What could Aditi do to keep her pride healthy?
qa.a: Keep thanking her teammates and being kind to opponents, taking pride in her effort rather than showing off.

qa.q: How might Ishita have felt when Aditi praised her saves?
qa.a: Comforted a little, since she almost smiled, though she probably still felt sad about losing.

grounding: A child wins and feels wonderful, thanks her team and is kind to the losing goalkeeper instead of gloating.

passage:
"So how did the chess match go?" Urmila asked, ladling dal.
"I crushed Kunal! Checkmate in twenty moves! I told him to stick to snakes and ladders." Sumit grinned.
"You said that to his face?"
"Everyone laughed."
"Did Kunal?"
Sumit stopped, spoon halfway up. "No. He left early. He didn't even look at me."
"Was it sweet?"
"For a minute. Then kind of empty. Ishaan didn't clap either."
"You may play Kunal again, beta."
"He might beat me next time."
"And what would you want him to do then?"
Sumit put down his spoon. "Say well played. I'll tell him that tomorrow. 😊"

qa.q: How many moves did Sumit say the checkmate took?
qa.a: Twenty moves.

qa.q: What was Sumit feeling when Urmila asked whether Kunal laughed?
qa.a: Uncomfortable and a little ashamed: he stopped with his spoon halfway and admitted the win felt empty.

qa.q: What could Sumit do tomorrow to repair things with Kunal?
qa.a: Tell Kunal "well played," as he says he will.

qa.q: How might Kunal have felt when Sumit teased him?
qa.a: Hurt and embarrassed, since he left early and did not look at Sumit.

grounding: After beating his rival, the child shows off and rubs it in, finds it sweet for a moment but empty, and resolves to be gracious.
